import gin                                                                                                                                           
import tensorflow as tf                                                                                                                              
                                                                                                                                                     
from official.common import distribute_utils                                                                                                         
from official.common import flags as tfm_flags                                                                                                       
from official.core import task_factory                                                                                                               
from official.core import train_lib                                                                                                                  
from official.core import train_utils                                                                                                                
from official.modeling import performance                                                                                                            
from official.vision import registry_imports  # pylint: disable=unused-import                                                                        
from official.vision.utils import summary_manager                                                                                                    
                                                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                     
FLAGS = flags.FLAGS                                                                                                                                  
                                                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                                                     
def _run_experiment_with_preemption_recovery(params, model_dir): 
  """Runs experiment and tries to reconnect when encounting a preemption."""
  keep_training = True
  while keep_training:
    preemption_watcher = None
    try:
      distribution_strategy = distribute_utils.get_distribution_strategy(
          distribution_strategy=params.runtime.distribution_strategy,
          all_reduce_alg=params.runtime.all_reduce_alg,
          num_gpus=params.runtime.num_gpus,
          tpu_address=params.runtime.tpu)
      with distribution_strategy.scope():
        task = task_factory.get_task(params.task, logging_dir=model_dir)
      preemption_watcher = tf.distribute.experimental.PreemptionWatcher()

      train_lib.run_experiment(
          distribution_strategy=distribution_strategy,
          task=task,
          mode=FLAGS.mode,
          params=params,
          model_dir=model_dir,
          summary_manager=None,
          eval_summary_manager=summary_manager.maybe_build_eval_summary_manager(
              params=params, model_dir=model_dir
          ),
      )

      keep_training = False
    except tf.errors.OpError as e:
      if preemption_watcher and preemption_watcher.preemption_message:
        preemption_watcher.block_until_worker_exit()
        logging.info(
            'Some TPU workers had been preempted (message: %s), '
            'retarting training from the last checkpoint...',
            preemption_watcher.preemption_message)
        keep_training = True
      else:

def main(_):
  gin.parse_config_files_and_bindings(FLAGS.gin_file, FLAGS.gin_params)
  params = train_utils.parse_configuration(FLAGS)
  model_dir = FLAGS.model_dir
  if 'train' in FLAGS.mode:

    # may race against the train job for writing the same file.
    train_utils.serialize_config(params, model_dir)

  # Sets mixed_precision policy. Using 'mixed_float16' or 'mixed_bfloat16'
  # can have significant impact on model speeds by utilizing float16 in case of
  # GPUs, and bfloat16 in the case of TPUs. loss_scale takes effect only when
  # dtype is float16
  if params.runtime.mixed_precision_dtype:
    performance.set_mixed_precision_policy(params.runtime.mixed_precision_dtype)

  _run_experiment_with_preemption_recovery(params, model_dir)
  train_utils.save_gin_config(FLAGS.mode, model_dir)

if __name__ == '__main__':
  tfm_flags.define_flags()
  flags.mark_flags_as_required(['experiment', 'mode', 'model_dir'])
  app.run(main)

github.author: realharryhero

comments.author: ChandniJha630
comments.body: Assign me this issue I would love to contribute

comments.author: 3zhang
comments.body:
Not a complete fix but a workaround:
Run matplotlib inline immediately **after** tensorflow_models imported:
````
import tensorflow_models as tfm
%matplotlib inline
````
Then every time you use plt to plot, make sure to add plt.show() at the end like:
````
plt.plot([1,2,3])
plt.show()
````
plt.show() is necessary to let the plot show up.

comments.author: bharatjetti
comments.body: Hi @realharryhero Glad that you found a fix, I have reproduced the issue,in this case when we are using matplotlib in notebook, the backend doesn't have GUI to display the plots, so that is the reason we need to explicitly get backends like `Qt5Agg` or `TkAgg`, as mentioned by @3zhang magic function like `%matplotlib inline` also does the job. While using complex libraries like TensorFlow which have multi threaded optimized computations can sometimes conflict the backend so if we follow the correct import order, we can avoid this issue. Here is the screenshot.

comments.body:
I am experiencing the same issue. I tested a lot of different scenarios though. I read [faq.md](https://github.com/tensorflow/models/blob/master/research/object_detection/g3doc/faq.md) and based on this I found in protos default values set 100 which I changed to 1000 and trained the model without any change though.

I also trained my model and scored high mAP 0.7 using classic CLI command with main_tf2.py and --checkpoint_dir and then run tensorboard and tensorboard for evaluationf always shows only 100 groundtruth used bounding boxes for each images. I suppose based on faq.md it also uses only 100 bboxes also for training and remaining bboxes are clipped and not used during the training. What I dont know is where / how to force TF2 objection detection API to use more 100 bboxes per image in trainig. comments.author: Sam-Seaberry
comments.body:
The error you are seeing with only 100 ground truth is due to a missing pipeline.config parameter. Tensorflow will default to the lowest BB number its given, so if you have haven't set one of the inputs to greater than 100 it will only ever display 100. 

This is noted here https://github.com/tensorflow/models/blob/master/research/object_detection/protos/input_reader.proto line 111

The Protos folder gives information about what each section of your pipeline.config can/does accept, if there is a variable in a protos file that links to the max number of detection or bounding boxes that you do not set in your pipeline.config add it.

For example: post_processing.proto has variables: `max_total_detections` and `max_detections_per_class` if these are missing from your pipeline.config post_processing section you will get unwanted results (for images with over 100 detections per image/class).

Please read my initial comment in full. From a quick look I can see you are missing:

 `max_number_of_boxes: 500` should be in your eval_input_reader section.

`max_number_of_boxes: 500` should be under train_input_reader

comments.author: Sam-Seaberry
comments.body:
I found the source of the error:
The eval_input_reader is repeated and so when writing to it you must specify the index. causing this :
`pipeline_config.eval_input_reader.max_number_of_boxes = 500`
To throw an error. 

To solve simple add an index to the call:
`pipeline_config.eval_input_reader[0].max_number_of_boxes = 500`

Hi @JunHyungKang,

Thanks for providing the colab code. We suggest you to once go through this [tutorial](https://www.tensorflow.org/tfmodels/vision/object_detection) how to configure a object detection pipeline. Instead of that you can load the experiment configuration using  this line `exp_config = exp_factory.get_exp_config('retinanet_resnetfpn_coco')`. Which will load the configuration required for `retinanet_resnetfpn_coco`.

Now you can access the experiment configuration like an object and change all required variables in the configuration and use it for training your model with custom dataset and custom configuration. Please use `distribution_strategy.scope()` so that it will take care of the distribution strategy.

Please check this [gist](https://colab.research.google.com/gist/sineeli/c738f3394194b3d53b3b811f38b3eaa1/10947.ipynb) which gives a glimpse how you can modify the configuration and make use of it to fuller extent. 

There may be new commits in git clone which are not yet in stable release, we suggest you to you use pip install so that if there are any on going errors/bugs, they will not be any problems to your training. I hope this will help you resolve the issue.


Thanks

comments.body: Hi @JunHyungKang, Please make sure to follow below requirements while creating `tfrecords`. 'image/encoded' | bytes | Required. The encoded image bytes. -- | -- | -- 'image/source_id' | string | Required. The unique identifier of the image, need to be an number in string. 'image/height' | integer | Optional. The height of the image. If not exisit, inferred from image. 'image/width' | integer | Optional. The width of the image. If not exisit, inferred from image. 'image/object/bbox/xmin' | a list of float | Required. The normalized xmin coordinates of all the instances. 'image/object/bbox/xmax' | a list of float | Required. The normalized xmax coordinates of all the instances. 'image/object/bbox/ymin' | a list of float | Required. The normalized ymin coordinates of all the instances. 'image/object/bbox/ymax' | a list of float | Required. The normalized ymax coordinates of all the instances. 'image/object/class/label' | a list of integer | Required. The class indices of all the instances. Note that 0 is reserved for background. 'image/object/mask' | a list of bytes | Optional. The mask of all the instances in PNG format. 'image/object/area' | a list of float | Optional. The area of all the instances. If not exisit, derived from the bounding boxes. 'image/object/is_crowd' | a list of integer | Optional. The 0/1 integers to denote whether instances are a crowd. The crowd instance get special treatement during the evaluation. 0 (not crowd) by default. The dummy records you provided has a error while evaluation because the source_id has string data with alphbatic characters in it. Please find the [gist](https://colab.sandbox.google.com/gist/sineeli/cd42367449e2eae0687ae3e252df9c3a/10947.ipynb) which I am trying to debug. Also add the classes as 2 because the classes start from 0 in general in the cooc_json. Which can be considered as background if I am not wrong. Please check the below screenshot from [BCCD](https://public.roboflow.com/object-detection/bccd) dataset. Please go through this object detection [tutorial](https://www.tensorflow.org/tfmodels/vision/object_detection) if you have not gone through, it uses BCCD dataset and trains the model. Still if the error persists, once you are ready with proper tfrecords format, we are happy to debug and further help you to resolve the issue. Thanks

comments.body:
@milesial Thank you for quick reply. 

You're right.  I lacked understanding of the original paper.  

My purpose is to break the symmetric in the +z direction in pointcloud classification (SE3-transformer +z in the SE3-transformer work).     
I thought this idea would be implemented through a method similar to the way mentioned above.

Even if the meaning is wrong in the QM9 dataset, I wanted to make sure that the SE3-transformer works normally by making the shape of the input the same.

Your comment made me think deeply about this work. Thank you.

comments.author: milesial
comments.body:
Yes, for point cloud experiments using +z, I suggest data loading code like this:

```
G = dgl.transform.knn_graph(points, self.num_neighbors + 1)
G = dgl.transform.remove_self_loop(G)
src, dst = G.edges()
absolute_z = points[:, -1]

# position relative to neighbors
relative_pos = points[src] - points[dst]
relative_z = relative_pos[:, -1].clone()
relative_pos_no_z = relative_pos.clone()
relative_pos_no_z[:, -1] = 0
feat = torch.stack([relative_pos, relative_pos_no_z], dim=1)
edge_feats = {'0': relative_z[..., None, None], '1': feat}
node_feats = {'0': absolute_z[..., None, None]}
G.edata['rel_pos'] = points[dst] - points[src]

return G, node_feats, edge_feats, label
```

With the model defined with:
```
fiber_in=Fiber({0: 1}),
fiber_edge=Fiber({0: 1, 1: 2}),
```

That way you have two 3D edge features: one vector and one vector with z=0. You also have one 1D edge feature: the relative z component. You have one 1D node feature: the absolute z component.

You can find more insight in this discussion about ScanObjectNN https://github.com/FabianFuchsML/se3-transformer-public/issues/13

github.author: okyanusoz

comments.author: Tylman-M
comments.body:
This is how I fixed it for my code. I highly suspect there's a better way to fix this, but in short three things needed to be fixed:

1. Change 'end_token_id' to 'stop_token_ids'
2. Wrap the token id argument in a list
3. add '.to_tensor()' to the encoder input tokens'



(Note, I extended mine from Spanish only to French, so my encoders are named "fr_..." instead of "spa_")
```
def decode_sequences(input_sentences):
    batch_size = 1

    # Tokenize the encoder input.
    encoder_input_tokens = ops.convert_to_tensor(eng_tokenizer(input_sentences))
    if len(encoder_input_tokens[0]) < MAX_SEQUENCE_LENGTH:
        pads = ops.full((1, MAX_SEQUENCE_LENGTH - len(encoder_input_tokens[0])), 0)
        #encoder_input_tokens = ops.concatenate([encoder_input_tokens.to_tensor(), pads], 1) # <-- Original
        encoder_input_tokens = ops.concatenate([encoder_input_tokens.to_tensor(), pads], 1) # <-- Add ".to_tensor()" at the base of this

    # Define a function that outputs the next token's probability given the
    # input sequence.
    def next(prompt, cache, index):
        logits = transformer([encoder_input_tokens, prompt])[:, index - 1, :]
        # Ignore hidden states for now; only needed for contrastive search.
        hidden_states = None
        return logits, hidden_states, cache

    # Build a prompt of length 40 with a start token and padding tokens.
    length = 40
    start = ops.full((batch_size, 1), fr_tokenizer.token_to_id("[START]"))
    pad = ops.full((batch_size, length - 1), fr_tokenizer.token_to_id("[PAD]"))
    prompt = ops.concatenate((start, pad), axis=-1)

    generated_tokens = nlp.samplers.GreedySampler()(
        next,
        prompt,
        # end_token_id = fr_tokenizer.token_to_id("[END]") #<-- Original
        stop_token_ids=[fr_tokenizer.token_to_id("[END]")], #<-- Change argument name and wrap in list
        index=1,  # Start sampling after start token.
    )
    generated_sentences = fr_tokenizer.detokenize(generated_tokens)
    return generated_sentences
```

github.author: Paryavi

comments.author: Paryavi
comments.body:
Colab AI suggests this;

Colab AI
The error is coming from the keras_cv.metrics.object_detection.box_coco_metrics module. The _box_concat function is expecting two tensors with the same shape, but the shapes of the tensors in your input are not the same. The first tensor has a shape of [4, 2, 4], while the second tensor has a shape of [4, 1, 4].

To fix this error, you need to make sure that the two tensors have the same shape. One way to do this is to use the tf.expand_dims function to add a new dimension to the second tensor. For example, you could use the following code:

 
tf.expand_dims(val_ds, axis=1)
[Use code with caution](https://g.co/legal/generative-code)
This will add a new dimension to the second tensor, making it have the same shape as the first tensor. Once you have done this, you should be able to run the yolo.fit function without any errors.

github.title: `init_range_low` is not adhered to in recent release
github.author: cathaloruaidh

comments.author: ahmedfgad
comments.body:
In version 3.4.0, the mutation was applied by:
1. Generating a random mutation value.
2. Changing the data type of the random value and rounding it if necessary. 
3. Summing the gene value to the random value.
4. Changing the data type again.

For example:
1. The random value is sampled be default from the -1 to 1 range. 
2. If the random value is 0.5 and you used the `int` data type, then it changes to 0.
3. The new random value 0 is added to the gene value. If the gene value is 0 or 1, then it keeps the same value.

Note that the values are sampled from the -1 to 1 range. It might happen that the random value is -1. In this case, -1 is added to 0 and the new gene value will be `-1` which is outside the `init_range_low` to `init_range_high` range. You were just lucky.

In version 3.5.0, the behaviour changed to:
1. Generate a random mutation value.
2. Summing the gene value to the random value.
3. Changing the data type of the random value and rounding it if necessary. 

For example:
1. The random value could be -1.
2. The random value -1 is added to the gene value (e.g. 0) and the result is -1.
3. The data type of the new gene value -1 is changed. The new value keeps -1.

If the gene value is -1 and you again sampled a random value of -1, then the new gene value becomes -2. The process repeats to increase the magnitude of the gene value until it reaches the values you found such as -14.

This is the new working code. Instead of using `init_range_low` to `init_range_high`, just use the `gene_space` parameter.
```python
import pygad
import numpy
import scipy

def fitness_func(ga_instance, solution, solution_idx):
	fitness = numpy.sum(solution[0::2]) - numpy.sum(solution[1::2])
	return fitness

fitness_function = fitness_func
num_generations = 2
num_parents_mating = 10

sol_per_pop = 100
num_genes = 20

gene_type=int
# init_range_low = 0
# init_range_high = 2
gene_space = [0, 1]

parent_selection_type = "sss"
keep_parents = 10

crossover_type = "scattered"
mutation_type = "random"
mutation_percent_genes = 100 / num_genes

ga_instance = pygad.GA(num_generations=num_generations,
num_parents_mating=num_parents_mating,
fitness_func=fitness_function,
sol_per_pop=sol_per_pop,
num_genes=num_genes,
gene_type=gene_type,
# init_range_low=init_range_low,
# init_range_high=init_range_high,
gene_space=gene_space,
parent_selection_type=parent_selection_type,
keep_parents=keep_parents,
crossover_type=crossover_type,
mutation_type=mutation_type,
mutation_percent_genes=mutation_percent_genes)

ga_instance.run()

solution, solution_fitness, solution_idx = ga_instance.best_solution()
print("Parameters of the best solution : {solution}".format(solution=solution))
print("Fitness value of the best solution = {solution_fitness}".format(solution_fitness=solution_fitness))

prediction = numpy.sum(solution[0::2]) - numpy.sum(solution[1::2])
print("Predicted output based on the best solution : {prediction}".format(prediction=prediction))
```

Hi Luke,

> I was surprised that einops.reduce and einops.rearrange does not handle this case. 

```
einops.reduce('b c h w -> b c') averages over h w

github.title: Issue loading remote source code offline?
github.author: brendanartley

comments.author: tomaarsen
comments.body:
Hello!

It is possible, but you have to make some modifications. Because the remote model itself requires modeling files that are in another remote location, we can't use `local_files_only=True` to only use cached files, as although we'd use the local files from the model itself, it would still require downloading the modeling files from another remote location.

Here are the steps to get it working locally without internet:
1. Save the model locally:
   ```python
   from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

   model = SentenceTransformer("nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v1", trust_remote_code=True)
   model.save_pretrained("nomic-embed-text-v1-local")
   ```
2. Observe the `config.json` of the downloaded model and search for `auto_map`. This will be a mapping of autoclass names to either `{repository}--{file}.{class}` or `{file}.{class}`. Either way, we want to download all files mentioned in this mapping. Place them in the local model repository.
3. If the `config.json` `auto_map` has the format of `{repository}--{file}.{class}`, update it to `{file}.{class}` instead. We have the files in the same directory as the config now, so this should work.
4. Load the model "like normal", but with `local_files_only=True`: 
   ```python
   embedding_model = SentenceTransformer(
       "nomic-embed-text-v1-local", 
       trust_remote_code=True,
       local_files_only=True,
   )
   ```
P.s. I'm not sure if `trust_remote_code=True` is still necessary - it might not be, feel free to experiment.

- Tom Aarsen

github.author: Optimox

comments.author: johnnv1
comments.body:
Thanks for the report, I will update the docs

my interpretation is that they have different behaviors, I think the most appropriate here would be to add as an extra option or even as a new augmentation. As a side note, this function "just" uses `torch.nn.functional.pad`.

cc: @shijianjian

comments.author: Optimox
comments.body:
Yes I agree that `PadTo` does not have to be similar to `PadIfNeeded` however returning the upper left corner without any warning of any form does not seem right to me.

The problem comes from this line : https://github.com/kornia/kornia/blob/3bf798ee6d5e1cfdb1dcca2fa7959e6acd3007b1/kornia/augmentation/_2d/geometric/pad.py#L68 which can create a negative `height_pad`. I actually find it strange that `torch.nn.functional.pad` accepts that.

If it can help here is a sketch of what I would expect from `PadIfNeeded` (please note that there is no correct docstring, the inverse_tranform is not implemented and I don't know what is wrong with apply transform method). Also I slightly changed the behavior of the padding to get a central image as it seems more natural to me to center the original image:

```
from typing import Any, Dict, Optional, Tuple, Union, cast
from kornia.augmentation._2d.geometric.base import GeometricAugmentationBase2D
from torch import Tensor
import torch
class PadIfNeeded(GeometricAugmentationBase2D):
    r"""Pad the given sample to a specific size only if needed.
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        size: Tuple[int, int],
        pad_mode: str = "constant",
        pad_value: Union[int, float] = 0,
        keepdim: bool = False,
        return_transform: Optional[bool] = None,
    ) -> None:
        super().__init__(p=1.0, return_transform=return_transform, same_on_batch=True, p_batch=1.0, keepdim=keepdim)
        self.flags = dict(size=size, pad_mode=pad_mode, pad_value=pad_value)

    # REMARK: I don't know what those TODOs are but it's worth doing them:)
    # TODO: It is incorrect to return identity
    # TODO: Having a resampled version with ``warp_affine``
    def compute_transformation(self, image: Tensor, params: Dict[str, Tensor], flags: Dict[str, Any]) -> Tensor:
        return self.identity_matrix(image)

    def apply_transform(
        self, input: Tensor, params: Dict[str, Tensor], flags: Dict[str, Any], transform: Optional[Tensor] = None
    ) -> Tensor:
        _, _, height, width = input.shape

        height_pad: int = max(flags["size"][0] - height, 0)
        width_pad: int = max(flags["size"][1] - width, 0)
        
        # center the padding
        left_width: int = width_pad // 2
        right_width: int = width_pad - left_width
            
        top_height: int = height_pad // 2
        bottom_height: int = height_pad - top_height
            
        return torch.nn.functional.pad(
            input, [left_width, right_width, top_height, bottom_height], mode=flags["pad_mode"], value=flags["pad_value"]
        )

    def inverse_transform(
        self,
        input: Tensor,
        flags: Dict[str, Any],
        transform: Optional[Tensor] = None,
        size: Optional[Tuple[int, int]] = None,
    ) -> Tensor:
        size = cast(Tuple[int, int], size)
        raise NotImplementedError
```

In my view, I think it would be a case of just adding it as a note in the documentation. And if Jian thinks it's ok we could update it so that the padding is the same for all sides (for me is also the most natural scenario).

Thank you once again for your support. Your explanation was instrumental in helping me understand and resolve the issue.

comments.author: littlebullGit
comments.body:
## The reported issue stems from how callbacks are passed to [LightningCLI]src/lightning/pytorch/cli.py's `trainer_defaults` parameter. This did not seems an issue for the mix imports. 
@tonyzamyatin @mauvilsa @oseymour @SkafteNicki 

### Root Cause
The `callbacks` parameter in `trainer_defaults` expects **instances** of callbacks (e.g., `[MyCallback()]`), not the class itself (`[MyCallback]`). 

### Testing Results
Below is a test script to verify this behavior across different PyTorch Lightning versions (2.5.0 and 2.8.0). 
```python
# Test 1: Passing callback class - THIS WILL FAIL (expected)
try:
    cli = MyCLI(
        BoringModel,
        BoringDataModule,
        trainer_defaults={
            "callbacks": [MyCallback],  # Passing class (incorrect)
            "max_epochs": 1,
        },
        run=False
    )
    print("Test 1 PASSED: Successfully created CLI with callback class")
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Test 1 FAILED: {type(e).__name__}: {str(e)}")

# Test 2: Passing callback instance - THIS WILL PASS
try:
    cli = MyCLI(
        BoringModel,
        BoringDataModule,
        trainer_defaults={
            "callbacks": [MyCallback()],  # Passing instance (correct)
            "max_epochs": 1,
        },
        run=False
    )
    print("Test 2 PASSED: Successfully created CLI with callback instance")
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Test 2 FAILED: {type(e).__name__}: {str(e)}")
```
```output
Test 1 FAILED: ValueError: Expected a parent
Test 2 PASSED: Successfully created CLI with callback instance

```

@ishaaq I wrote all below and then I just though, what pytorch ver are you using? I just tried `torch.load(..., weights_only=True)` on a recent train checkpoint (loaded in pytorch 2.5, train was using 2.2 I think). It worked.

There were a number of late additions to safe globals defaults in pytorch as this change evolved on their end. I don't feel we're saving any funky types in our train checkpoints by default, so curious what it's breaking on or if pytorch 2.5 fixes it?

----
pretrained model weights are hosted and distributed online, training checkpoints are artifacts of your own training that were generated locally (though they could be shared, we don't distribute them). So the 'resume' functionality expects to be operating on the output of your own local training.

github.title: Inconsistent shape resolution scope when using dataclasses
github.author: jpthalman

comments.author: patrick-kidger
comments.body:
This is intended. jaxtyping only sees the type hint you've written directly in-line, which in this case is `Vector`. It will then essentially do `isinstance(..., Vector)`, which passes. Job done. This is normal Python behaviour, `isinstance` against a class is 'shallow' and doesn't try to recursively check every sub-object contained within the class.

I think the behaviour you're after here is obtainable, though! You'd need to override `type(Vector).__instancecheck__` so that the `isinstance` will only pass if `isinstance(v.x, Vector.x) and isinstance(v.y, Vector.y)`.

Finally I'd note that you're using `chex.dataclass`. If you're here and using the Equinox ecosystem then you might like [`equinox.Module`](https://github.com/patrick-kidger/equinox), which is similar but fixes several footguns too. (Inheritance, bound methods, new stuff like abstract variables, ...)

I hope that helps!

>

Well, it isn't impossible. If m_1 is not used in the optimal plan, it is possible to compute the optimal plan without relying on something like `m_1+m_2-m_1==m_2`. As you mentioned in a previous comment, even a cost of +inf could work (the fact that it can currently output something that isn't even a transport plan is a bit alarming). We will handle truly infinite values separately in Gudhi (it is currently officially unsupported), so hopefully our users won't be tempted to simulate infinity with large values...

comments.body:
The entropy has a weird impact that it will promote creation of mass which for unbalanced is  a bit counter intuitive. For instance the mass of the plan can be greater than the mass of each of the marginals... It was not the standard in any of the unalanced papers to the bets of my knowledge and we originally implemented is to have similar regularization than sinkhorn paper but it wa sprobably a bad idea.

When using the KL you shrink toward the rank one plan (of mass 1 if both marginals sum to 1) so there is no creation of mass.

github.title: PAR DiagnosticReport not 1.0 with float categorical columns
github.author: frances-h

comments.author: npatki
comments.body:
### Workaround

If anyone is running into this, here is a suggested workaround:

1. Identify any `categorical` columns (in the metadata) that are actually represented as numbers in your data (ints, floats, etc.)
2. Cast these columns as objects before inputting them into the PARSynthesizer.
3. At the end when you get synthetic data, cast them back as ints, floats, etc.

Here is a code snippet that accomplishes the below. Replace the list `CAT_COLUMN_NAMES` with the list of your column names.

```python
CAT_COLUMN_NAMES = ['ColA', 'ColB', ... ]

data = <your pandas DataFrame>
metadata = <your SingleTableMetadata object>

# cast the categorical columns to strings
for col_name in CAT_COLUMN_NAMES:
  data[col_name] = data[col_name].astype('object')

# now proceed with modeling and sampling as usual
synthesizer = PARSynthesizer(metadata)
synthesizer.fit(data)
synthetic_data = synthesizer.sample(num_sequences=10)

# (optional) cast the categorical columns back to floats
for col_name in CAT_COLUMN_NAMES:
  try:
    synthetic_data[col_name] = synthetic_data[col_name].astype('float')
  except:
    print('Column name', col_name, 'could not be converted back to a float')
    continue
```

github.author: gabriellestein

comments.author: AngledLuffa
comments.body:
This is kinda funny.  The tokenizer has misinterpreted `Johanna` to be similar to tokens such as `wanna` and `gonna`, which get split into `want to` and `going to`.  I suppose in this case it would be `Johan to`?  Obviously this is incorrect, and I will add a sentence or two to the training data to hopefully fix it up.

To answer the question regarding not having an `xpos`, the tokens which are split into multiple word pieces are included in the `to_dict()` result like this.  Those macro tokens don't have POS because they are composed of multiple words, so for example `want to` both have their own POS in the above example.  You can skip them if they have an ID which isn't a single integer, or you can iterate over just the word pieces with `doc.sentences[i].words()`

Going through the English words ending with "nna", here are some broken examples:

```
My favorite actress is Joanna Lumley
I used a burnt sienna crayon to color in the picture
A large goanna bit my arm
Someone I know wears a bandanna every time he goes dancing
Legend tells us belladonna killed Socrates
Ms. Bumbry was never afraid to inhabit the primadonna role offstage
Unlike most fish, channa can leave the water for a short period of time
Apparently Madonna loathes hydrangeas
The savanna has many lions
I got a henna tattoo of my Chinese name
The Israelites survived on manna during the Exodus
That restaurant has excellent panna cotta
Nanna is an Icelandic singer
```

Correctly not split:

```
I accidentally touched Jennifer's antenna and she accused me of sexual harassment
The common platanna is invasive in the US
The music at the feiseanna was energizing
Gloria, hosanna in excelsis
The Duenna is an opera in three acts
I have not read Anna Karenina
A pinna is a fern leaf
One set of Islamic traditions is the sunna
You were supposed to take ONE senna, not ten.  Now who's going to clean up all this ...
```


Correctly split, but the lemmatizer gets it wrong - presumably no training data available - 

```
Dinna light that candle!
```

should split to "do not"

Then there's the ambiguous case of `canna`, which is either a lily or Scotty saying "I canna change the laws of physics!"

Heh, THREE Star Trek references in one github response.  I'm becoming more efficient!

### Root caused

The Bug

  In deploy/docker/auth.py:

  2. Lines 34-35 in verify_token:

comments.author: rflamary
comments.body:
yes that's it good catch! basically we cannot solve the problem precisely if there exist two values different values in m such that m_1+_2=m_1 due to numerical precision.

I dont' think we can say it is a bug or something we can solve if it is due to the numerical precision for float64.

Maybe we can add a warning when the dynamic in M is too large. Note that if you want to forbid a link you just need to set its value to M.max()*1.0001 or something like that instead of a very large value, it will not change the solution or the value.

Again thank you for reporting this weird behavior.

comments.author: mglisse
comments.body:
> yes that's it good catch! basically we cannot solve the problem precisely if there exist two values different values in m such that m_1+_2=m_1 due to numerical precision.
> 
> I dont' think we can say it is a bug or something we can solve if it is due to the numerical precision for float64.

Well, it isn't impossible. If m_1 is not used in the optimal plan, it is possible to compute the optimal plan without relying on something like `m_1+m_2-m_1==m_2`. As you mentioned in a previous comment, even a cost of +inf could work (the fact that it can currently output something that isn't even a transport plan is a bit alarming). Depending on the algorithm, arranging the computations to be robust like that can be trivial or very complicated and costly, and the question is whether it is worth the trouble. Maybe it isn't here...

> Maybe we can add a warning when the dynamic in M is too large. Note that if you want to forbid a link you just need to set its value to M.max()*1.0001 or something like that instead of a very large value, it will not change the solution or the value.

Just around the max of the other values may not be sufficient to forbid a link, it could still be used to transport a small mass in the optimal plan.
We will handle truly infinite values separately in Gudhi (it is currently officially unsupported), so hopefully our users won't be tempted to simulate infinity with large values...

comments.author: rflamary
comments.body:
POT exact OT solver is a wrapper around the C++ LEMON solver and we modifying it is out of what we can do. In addition, it might require some kind of testings at each iteration that could greatly decrease the performance. 

About the max value, I think it is sufficient if the dynamic in M is limited (below 1e14 for instance) adding a cost that is bigger than all the other would prevent any mass on the link because the solver is a Network simplex and the solution will always be on a face of the polytop and under the dynamic condition this face can be improved if there is mass on the largest values of M.

Hi,
The default behavior is now with the KL regularization instead of the entropy. If you add `reg_type="entropy"`, you should recover the result of the 0.9.4 version.

```

>>> a = [0.5, 0.5]
>>> b = [0.5, 0.5]
>>> M = [[0, 1], [1, 0]]
>>> ot.unbalanced.sinkhorn_knopp_unbalanced(a, b, M, 1, 1, reg_type="entropy")

       [0.18807032, 0.51122814]])
```

comments.author: atong01
comments.body:
Hi Clément,

Thank you! May I ask why this changed and / or why it is preferred?

I don't really have a preference but this seems to change (somewhat significantly?) a number of my projects and it would be nice to know what I should be using.

Thanks,
Alex

comments.author: rflamary
comments.body:
The entropy has a weird impact that it will promote creation of mass which for unbalanced is  a bit counter intuitive. For instance the mass of the plan can be greater than the mass of each of the marginals... It was not the standard in any of the unalanced papers to the bets of my knowledge and we originally implemented is to have similar regularization than sinkhorn paper but it wa sprobably a bad idea.

When using the KL you shrink toward the rank one plan (of mass 1 if both marginals sum to 1) so there is no creation of mass.

github.title: Calling eqx.Module method invokes user defined __getattr__
github.author: yuzu-ido

comments.author: patrick-kidger
comments.body:
So as a general Python thing (unrelated to JAX or Equinox) it's usually inadvisible to have a wildcard `__getattr__` that attempts to handle everything. It's pretty common for any code you interact with try to try doing something like:
```python
if hasattr(your_obj, "__some_magic_method__"):
    your_obj.__some_magic_method__(...)
```
which will give unexpected behaviour here!

In this case you're running afoul of exactly this kind of thing in Equinox: we check for `__name__` and `__qualname__` attributes at various points internally (along with several other special attributes) to be sure that we can forward them appropriately e.g. across flattening+unflattening.

The best fix here would be to check the value of `name` in your `__getattr__`, and only handle the ones you know you want to handle.

An alternative would be to handle this case in particular by doing:
```python
if name in ("__name__", "__qualname__"):
    raise AttributeError
```

comments.author: yuzu-ido
comments.body: Thanks for the response. There's quite a lot of `name` I'd want to handle, so the alternative option sounds like a plan. My temporary fix was to copy and paste the ~10 line helper function into` __getattr__` directly but that seems cleaner.

github.title: An array-like defined with `eqx.Module` does not support `jnp.asarray` with the `__array__` method
github.author: gautierronan

comments.author: johannahaffner
comments.body:
Hi, 

this is because JAX handles arrays a bit differently, I think. If I switch to the magic method `__jax_array__`, it works. 
In that case, there is also no mix between `numpy` and `jax.numpy`, which don't always do the same thing under the hood and could potentially lead to confusing errata arising from their interactions. 

Here is the modified MWE, which now works: 

```python
import jax.numpy as jnp
import equinox as eqx
from jaxtyping import Array

class MyArray:
    def __init__(self, x):
        self.x = x

    def __jax_array__(self) -> Array:
        return self.x

class MyEqxArray(eqx.Module):
    x: Array

    def __jax_array__(self) -> Array:
        return self.x

x = MyArray(jnp.array([1, 2, 3]))
print(jnp.asarray(x))

y = MyEqxArray(jnp.array([1, 2, 3]))
print(jnp.asarray(y))
```

Depending on what purpose you want to extract arrays for, the `eqx.partition` and `eqx.combine` methods allow you to split models into array and non-array components, as described [here](https://docs.kidger.site/equinox/all-of-equinox/#2-filtering). 
I'm not quite sure what the best practice on magic methods is, though, since they are handled differently from regular methods, as Patrick stated [here](https://github.com/patrick-kidger/equinox/issues/770#issuecomment-2188003711).

Note: I've also switched to jaxtyping for the type annotation, but that should have no bearing on the errata avoided.

comments.author: johannahaffner
comments.body: PS: Take my recommendation with a few grains of salt, the future of `__jax_array__` [appears uncertain](https://github.com/jax-ml/jax/issues/10065). Way to fascinating for ordinary coffee breaks 😃

comments.author: patrick-kidger
comments.body:
Looks like this is because Equinox modules are trees, so they get flattened here:

https://github.com/jax-ml/jax/blob/1bc9df429d87920bdbbf874e84a63fbe3111e27d/jax/_src/numpy/lax_numpy.py#L5643

As Johanna highlights, I think `__array__` and `__jax_array__` should probably not be considered fully supported in JAX.

comments.author: gautierronan
comments.body:
Right, thanks for both of your answers. This issue about `__jax_array__` keeps coming up and is fairly annoying I have to say haha! Its lack of support is actually why I only implemented `__array__` in my example above.

I guess I should be raising a bug report in JAX, as the documentation of `jnp.asarray` does state explicity that a class with the `__array__` method should be supported as input.

Thanks @amifalk! There is indeed leakage here with the seed handler. I haven't been able to figure out why yet. Posting here for reference

```python
import numpyro
import numpyro.distributions as dist
import jax

def model():
    return numpyro.sample('a', dist.Normal(0, 1))    

def run(key):

comments.author: amifalk
fehiepsi
comments.body:
I think we figured it out. thanks for the examples!

seed(model) is an instance of a `seed` class which has mutable state. A fix for it is to close the seeded model into a function like
```
def seeded_model(*args, **kwargs):
    return seed(model, rng_seed=random.PRNGKey(0))(*args, **kwargs)
```
This way each time we call the model, a new instance of the seed handler will be created. Could you check if it works for your usage case? I'll think of a long term solution (maybe improve docstring for this).

github.author: Albly

comments.author: JeanKossaifi
comments.body:
Thank you @Albly for the clear issue and fix! This is a big bug!

A couple of notes: I tend to use the the relative reconstruction error as a metric as it is easily interpretable (`tl.norm(tensor - rec, 2)/tl.norm(tensor)`).

The other thing is that (besides the current bug!), the random tensor is typically full rank and so 1 < rank < 15 is likely to be very low. Which brings me to the last point: I would normally sample tensors using our random module:
```python
tl.random.random_tt(shape=tensor_shape, rank=20, dtype=np.complex128).to_tensor()
```

The issue is that in the complex context, it returns a complex tensor with 0 complex (which is why I suppose tests pass anyway). We could fix it but I feel this shouldn't be our responsibility to handle the core random generation but numpy/pytorch etc should do it however they want.

comments.author: MischaPanch
comments.body:
Pretty sure it's due to LazyFrames. The subproc module is full of assumptions, isinstance checks and whatnot, the dataflow is very implicit and everything is very poorly documented. It's old old code, before @opcode81 and I started to work on tianshou.

Here a summary of the data flow and the problem caused by LazyFrames created with help of AI:

Here’s the data flow and why LazyFrames breaks with the shared-memory worker:

Data flow with share_memory=True
- Buffer allocation (parent): Before starting the subprocess, the parent inspects the env’s observation_space and allocates a shared-memory buffer (ShArray) that exactly matches the observation’s dtype and shape. For FrameStack, that means a buffer sized for the stacked frames (e.g., [num_stack, H, W, C]).
- Acting and writing (child/subprocess):
  - On reset/step, the child computes the new observation and is supposed to write it into the shared buffer, then sends control data back through the pipe while replacing the observation payload with None.
  - The write is done by an encoder that traverses the observation structure and, at the leaves, writes only if the leaf is a NumPy ndarray.
- Reading (parent): Upon receiving the message (with None instead of the observation), the parent reconstructs the observation by reading from the shared-memory buffer.

What goes wrong with LazyFrames
- FrameStack returns a LazyFrames object, not a NumPy ndarray. It’s array-like and converts to an ndarray via np.asarray or __array__, but it does not satisfy isinstance(x, np.ndarray).
- The encoder’s leaf check is strict: it only writes to shared memory when the observation leaf is a real ndarray. Since LazyFrames is not an ndarray, the encoder skips the write entirely.
- The child still replaces the observation with None and signals completion. The parent then reads from the shared buffer expecting the “current” observation, but the buffer was never updated:
  - You read stale data (previous step/reset contents), uninitialized data, or zeros.
  - This causes off-by-one or inconsistent obs/obs_next relationships and test failures.
- Why np.stack “fixes” it: If you stack frames yourself with np.stack, you get a genuine ndarray. The encoder’s isinstance check passes, the write occurs, and everything works as intended.

Secondary considerations
- Shape and dtype are not the root cause here. The buffer is pre-sized from observation_space, which FrameStack updates to the stacked shape and dtype. LazyFrames would convert to that shape/dtype correctly if it were coerced to an ndarray before writing.
- The request–response protocol avoids races, but it cannot prevent “skipped write then decode” when the type check filters out non-ndarray array-likes.

Conceptual fix
- Ensure the child always materializes array-like observations (e.g., LazyFrames) to a NumPy array before writing to shared memory, e.g., by coercing with np.asarray at the encoder’s leaves. This retains the zero-copy benefit for true ndarrays and makes LazyFrames compatible.

Based on the provided logs, it is clear that the error is rooted at: `_get_lora_matrices` in `peft/tuners/vblora/layer.py`
```if self.training and vblora_logits_A[0, 0].isinf().any():```

I found a similar graph break here: https://thomasjpfan.com/2025/03/pytorch-graphs-three-ways-data-dependent-control-flow/

Typically, we want to use a tensorized control flow like:
```
torch._assert(
        torch.isfinite(vblora_logits_A[0, 0]).all(),
        "Found infinity values in VB-LoRA logits. Ensure training was not resumed from a `save_only_topk_weights` model."
    )
```

or perhaps using `torch.cond`

Once I know your versions, I can try to reproduce your environment more accurately and work on a concrete fix.

comments.author: tillahoffmann
comments.body:
This is an interesting one. I agree that we should probably cast to the appropriate dtype for the constraint of the parameter because the behavior can be surprising. E.g., passing an int covariance matrix to a multivariate normal leaves the passed parameter as int, but the Cholesky decomposition has floating dtype.

```python
In [1]: from numpyro import distributions as dists
        from jax import numpy as jnp

In [2]: def get_args(dist):
   ...:     return {key: getattr(dist, key, None) for key in dist.arg_constraints}
   ...: 

In [10]: get_args(dists.MultivariateNormal(0, jnp.ones((1, 1), dtype=int)))
Out[10]: 
{'loc': array([0]),
 'covariance_matrix': Array([[1]], dtype=int32),
 'precision_matrix': Array([[1.]], dtype=float32),
 'scale_tril': Array([[1.]], dtype=float32)}
```

Likewise, if we pass the precision matrix as int, it stays as int, but the cov matrix is float.

```python
In [11]: get_args(dists.MultivariateNormal(0, precision_matrix=jnp.ones((1, 1), dtype=int)))
Out[11]: 
{'loc': array([0]),
 'covariance_matrix': Array([[1.]], dtype=float32),
 'precision_matrix': Array([[1]], dtype=int32),
 'scale_tril': Array([[1.]], dtype=float32)}
```

I think we can derive the dtype unambiguously from the constraint?

comments.author: Sector14
comments.body:
I've run into the same issue, as a workaround until the issue linked above is resolved, if you quantise to 4bit nf4 via bitsandbytes everything appears to work (as long as you use guidance scale 0.0 for the turbo model).

fwiw I did try load_in_8bit=True rather than 4bit but that runs into an error:

`RuntimeError: view size is not compatible with input tensor's size and stride (at least one dimension spans across two contiguous subspaces). Use .reshape(...) instead.`

comments.author: hameerabbasi
comments.body: The above issue also contains another workaround. Good to know it's not my hardware.

comments.author: elinacse
comments.body:
@VikramRangarajan 
Looks like it's already fixed on main, just not in the release you're pinned to.

The crash happens because vllm/multimodal/video.py only caught ImportError around the torchcodec.decoders.VideoDecoder import. torchcodec raises a RuntimeError (not ImportError) when it can't load its native lib due to a CUDA mismatch, so it wasn't being caught and it took the whole process down at import time.

#47888 fixed this back on 2026-07-08 by widening the except to (ImportError, RuntimeError), so now a broken torchcodec install just falls back to a placeholder instead of crashing vllm serve. If you actually try to use the torchcodec backend it'll still fail with a proper error message, but it won't nuke startup anymore.

Problem is that fix merged after the v0.25.0 branch cut, so v0.25.0 doesn't have it. It is in v0.25.1 though (released today). Your pyproject.toml has vllm==0.24.0 pinned via wheels.vllm.ai, which is from before the fix even existed, so that lines up.

Bumping to vllm>=0.25.1 should get rid of the crash even though torchcodec still doesn't ship a cu129 wheel.

Thanks ,
Elina

github.title: [BUG] The behaviour of `param_groups_layer_decay()` towards `requires_grad==False` parameters
github.author: sjiang95

comments.author: rwightman
comments.body:
@sjiang95 so, I think I understand the issue but I believe this is the way it should be re consistency of behaviour and difficulty of implementation. 

I feel it makes most sense that the same 'groups' of params are assigned to the same lr scale regardless of which params are (externally) marked `requires_grad=False` by the user.

In the case you show, you marked all params of a group `requires_grad=False`. But it'd also be trivial to set a subset, like all norm layers, what then? The complexity of tracking partial/full state across groups and then adjusting at a group level, etc just seems to be overly complicated and likely more confusing for must users. 

In the typical use case of layer-wise LR decay the point is to focus on training the model towards the head and, if anything, have parts of the model near the stem/trunk frozen. So this also runs counter to the typical use case...  so in this exceptional case, I think the behaviour is reasonable? 

Does that make sense?

If any adjustment is to be made, maybe an addition to the API to set the 'anchor' or 'last group id' for the decay so in the case it's at the end we could say lr_scale 1.0 is applied at N-1. Dealing with any middle case would IMHO be not worth the effort.

comments.author: rwightman
comments.body:
This would be my proposal

```
  layer_max = num_layers - 1
  effective_layer_max = layer_max - layer_decay_offset
  layer_scales = [
      max(min_scale, layer_decay ** max(0, effective_layer_max - i))
      for i in range(num_layers)
  ]
```

  So with layer ids 0..3 and layer_decay=0.9:

  - layer_decay_offset=0 -> [0.729, 0.81, 0.9, 1.0]
  - layer_decay_offset=1 -> [0.81, 0.9, 1.0, 1.0]
  - layer_decay_offset=-1 -> [0.6561, 0.729, 0.81, 0.9]

comments.author: sjiang95
comments.body:
@rwightman , I finally solved this by implementing a customized callable `group_matcher()`.

Indeed

> but I believe this is the way it should be re consistency of behaviour and difficulty of implementation.

The lr decay mechanism is hard to be implemented in a general way to be compatible with arbitrary model architecture.

============================================================================

To anyone who is confused by how to implement a special param group parser,

besides the above-mentioned dict of re, another choice is to implement and return a callable with signature `foo(name: str)` by `group_matcher()`

https://github.com/huggingface/pytorch-image-models/blob/c769a585e0915c58fd7bb92f2355377aab7fc0e0/timm/models/_manipulate.py#L110-L114

For example,

https://github.com/huggingface/pytorch-image-models/blob/c769a585e0915c58fd7bb92f2355377aab7fc0e0/timm/models/cait.py#L351-L365

github.author: zhixiangli

comments.author: deependujha
comments.body:
Thanks for digging into this. The root cause is right: `root_device.index` is `None` on CPU, and torch ≥ 2.5 trips the "non-CPU accelerator" guard on that.

My hesitation is whether this is a path we should support. FSDP-on-CPU is gated above the strategy (accelerator blocks it, and FSDP requires `FSDPPrecision`), so there's no supported entry point where `parallel_devices` is `[cpu]`. The repro only reaches `_setup_model` by manually setting `_parallel_devices`/`_lightning_module`/`_process_group`, which reconstructs a state the framework never produces.

Worth noting too: `setup_environment` already encodes the opposite convention for CPU:

```python
kwargs["device_id"] = self.root_device if self.root_device.type != "cpu" else None
```

i.e. CPU → `None`. This PR flips that at the wrap call sites, so the same check would mean "pass `None`" in one place and "pass the device" in another.

On the test, since FSDP can't really run on CPU, mocking `FullyShardedDataParallel` is the only option, but that also means it only verifies the argument gets forwarded, for a config we otherwise reject. I can't think of anything meaningful that this lets us test"

My read is this should probably be closed as we don't have any concrete reason to support `FSDP-on-CPU`. Happy to be corrected if there's a use case I'm missing.

comments.author: zhixiangli
comments.body:
Thanks @deependujha — fair challenge, and the use case you're asking about is exactly why I filed this.

### The Use Case: CPU-Only Macrobenchmarking of Sharded-Checkpoint I/O

We are benchmarking the FSDP `state_dict_type="sharded"` checkpoint path against GCS (Google Cloud Storage) at an ~8B parameter scale. 

The primary metric under test is the **storage write/read pattern**: every rank writes its own shard concurrently to the same checkpoint directory. This simulates a realistic FSDP @ 8B write pattern, which DDP (which uses rank-0-only full writes) never exercises. 

We deliberately run this on a CPU-only fleet (using the `gloo` backend) because we are measuring object-storage I/O, not GPU compute. Since the `training_step` never actually forwards through the model, FSDP only touches the large parameters during initialization (sharding) and checkpointing. Pinning expensive GPUs to a pure storage-I/O benchmark would be highly wasteful and significantly harder to schedule in CI.

---

### The Workaround Today (Without This Fix)

To support this CPU-only benchmarking, we use a downstream `FSDPStrategy` subclass that bypasses the high-level GPU-only guards. However, because `root_device.index` is `None` on CPU, our subclass is forced to transiently monkeypatch `torch.distributed.fsdp.FullyShardedDataParallel` to rewrite `device_id=None` to `torch.device("cpu")` around the wrap call:

```python
class _CpuDeviceFSDP(orig_cls):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        if kwargs.get("device_id") is None:
            kwargs["device_id"] = torch.device("cpu")
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
```

While this works, it reaches into PyTorch internals and patches a module attribute that Lightning imports inside `_setup_model`. This is exactly the kind of fragile hack that this one-line upstream fix eliminates, allowing downstreams to cleanly extend `FSDPStrategy` for specialized testing/benchmarking.

---

### Addressing the "Inconsistent Convention"

I don't believe this introduces an inconsistent convention. The two `device_id` values feed into different PyTorch APIs with distinct contracts:

1. **`setup_environment` / `_setup_distributed`** -> `torch.distributed.init_process_group(device_id=...)`
   * Here, CPU correctly maps to `None` (adhering to the `c10d`/`gloo` contract).
2. **`setup_module` / `_setup_model`** -> `FullyShardedDataParallel(device_id=...)`
   * Here, PyTorch $\ge$ 2.5 rejects `None` on CPU and requires an explicit `torch.device("cpu")` to bypass the accelerator-detection guard.

Thus, using `None` in one place and the explicit device object in the other is necessary for each call to honor its respective PyTorch API contract. This PR does not alter the `setup_environment` convention.

---

### The Test Case

While mocking `FullyShardedDataParallel` only verifies argument forwarding, that is precisely the regression we need to prevent. The bug is that **Lightning passes FSDP a `device_id` that PyTorch rejects on CPU**. 

Asserting that the forwarded value is `torch.device("cpu")` on CPU (and the integer index on GPU) pins exactly this contract. The GPU path remains entirely unchanged, as the ternary operator only branches when the device type is `"cpu"`.

---

### Conclusion

Landing this fix allows downstream projects to drop fragile monkeypatches, enables cheaper CI/CD execution for checkpoint testing and storage-I/O benchmarking, and makes it easier to identify and implement further improvements in checkpointing performance.

comments.author: deependujha
comments.body:
Thanks @zhixiangli for the correction, you're right & it's not the inconsistency I initially thought.

That said, I still view this as a downstream extension scenario rather than an expansion of Lightning's supported CPU-FSDP surface; the sharded-checkpoint write pattern you're measuring lives in the checkpoint/save path, not in `FullyShardedDataParallel.__init__`. So I don't think this establishes FSDP-on-CPU as a supported target.

Where I've come around: as a robustness fix, it's a one-line change, near-zero maintenance, the GPU path is untouched (the branch only fires on `cpu`), and it aligns `device_id` with what torch ≥2.5 expects.

On that narrow basis, I'm fine with it, not as a statement that CPU is supported, but so a guard-bypassing subclass doesn't have to monkeypatch torch internals.

A short comment at the call site, noting CPU isn't a supported FSDP path (the branch only exists to honor the torch ≥2.5 contract), would keep future readers from reading support into it.

> The below seems to be a hack, to manage to save to safetensors.
> 
> ```python
> trainer.train()
> from torch.distributed.tensor import DTensor
> 
> state_dict = model.state_dict()

This doesn't work as `value.to_local()` gives you the local shard not the full tensor. comments.author: Craigacp
comments.body:
This works for me:
```python
from torch.distributed.checkpoint.state_dict import get_state_dict

state_dict, _ = get_state_dict(model, [])
# Coalesce the full state dict
for key, value in state_dict.items():
    if isinstance(value, DTensor):
        # materialize full tensor on each GPU
        local_full_value = value.full_tensor()
    else:
        local_full_value = value
    if accelerator.process_index == 0:
        # to avoid materializing the full model on CPU once per GPU we discard it if we're not the main process
        state_dict[key] = local_full_value.cpu()
accelerator.wait_for_everyone()
if accelerator.process_index == 0:
    model.save_pretrained(output_dir, state_dict, is_main_process=True)
accelerator.wait_for_everyone()
```

comments.author: eternalNight
comments.body:
I recently met the same issue on another model (qwen3.5-vl). The root cause in my case was that `self.embed_tokens(input_ids)` was followed by a graph break in a loop body in the same method, making torch dynamo skipping the whole method. During execution that method ran in eager mode **without** parameter gathering because DeepCompile had disabled it. As a result the `weight` was always shareded with a shape of `[0]`, leading to the error.

To confirm, you can enable dynamo logs by:

```python
import logging, torch
torch._logging.set_logs(dynamo=logging.INFO, graph_breaks=True)
torch._dynamo.config.verbose = True
```

and search for the following pattern in the logs:

```
Skipping frame because there is a graph break in a for/while loop
torch.compile intentionally decided to skip the frame xxx (/path/to/source line xxx) and fall back to eager.
```

Fixing that would require modifying the model implementation. In my case I need to separate the break-causing loop into a subroutine to work it around, e.g.

```python
#####
# Before
#####

def fast_pos_embed_interpolate(...):
    # The dynamic-data-dependent loop here
    ...
    pos_embeds = self.pos_embed(...)

#####
# After
#####

def fn(...):
    # The dynamic-data-dependent loop here

def fast_pos_embed_interpolate(...):
    xxx = fn(...)
    ...
    pos_embeds = self.pos_embed(...)
```

@zuoyanzhang For your case, you may first try a more recent version of transformers which seems to have the qwen2-moe model code simplified.

github.title: [Bug]: Gemma4 parser classifies plain output without channel markers differently in streaming and non-streaming mode
github.author: DavidDiao

comments.author: adesai-24
comments.body: Hello, I would love to take a crack at this bug, will being working on fixing this bug!

comments.author: lcw99
comments.body:
I independently hit the same root cause on `v0.25.0` with
`google/gemma-4-31B-it-qat-w4a16-ct` (reasoning + tool parser `gemma4`).
Confirming: `adjust_initial_state_from_prompt` unconditionally pre-inits
`REASONING` for any new-turn prompt (since `is_reasoning_end` returns `False`
on `<|turn>` when thinking is enabled), so channel-less direct answers stream
entirely as `reasoning` with empty `content`. The fix in this PR matches my
local reproduction — thanks for picking it up.

One related but SEPARATE bug this PR does not cover, which becomes visible
precisely after bug 1 is fixed (because normal text now correctly flows through
CONTENT): the `<turn|>` EOT token (and `<eos>`) can leak verbatim into the
streamed `content` field.

Root cause: `StreamingParserEngine._on_terminal` only drops these special
tokens (mapped to the internal `DROP_TERMINAL`) when they arrive WITH their
token ID in the same delta. In a streaming race where the detokenizer flushes
the token's text BEFORE its token ID reaches the parser, the text is lexed as
plain `CONTENT` and emitted as-is.

Minimal repro (no model/GPU needed):
```python
from vllm.parser.gemma4 import Gemma4Parser
# build parser with enable_thinking=True, feed a new-turn prompt tail
out = parser.parse_delta(
    "The answer is 4.<turn|>",          # text includes EOT
    token_ids_for("The answer is 4."),  # but token id for <turn|> NOT in this delta
    finished=True,
)
# -> content == "The answer is 4.<turn|>"   (leaked!)

I'm closing this issue because I have identified that this is the intended behavior. In my custom processor, I was wrapping the `LoRAAttnProcessor2_0` class. Since the `LoRAAttnProcessor2_0` class contains a destructive reassignment. I suggest adding a warning or `logger.info` in `LoRAAttnProcessor2_0` to inform users when this internal overwrite occurs, as it can be very difficult to debug -- I am happy to open a PR to add this logging if you think it would be a helpful addition to the library.

comments.author: VBS2004
comments.body: This looks already supported on main: the loop's pre-layer check is complemented by a post-loop capture right before the final norm — if self.end_layer in self.aux_hidden_state_layers: aux_hidden_states.append(hidden_states + residual) — so passing num_hidden_layers as a layer id yields the last layer's (pre-norm) output. This is documented in the Hidden State Extraction docs: https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/speculative_decoding/extract_hidden_states/ ("It is possible to save the last-layer's output hidden states by passing num_hidden_layers as a layer id"). Which vLLM version/commit are you on? Note the proposed idx + 1 change would shift the capture semantics for existing EAGLE3 layer ids, and appending after the last layer inside the loop can capture a sequence-parallel-sharded tensor under TP — the post-loop placement after the all-gather handles that.

comments.author: BenjaminBossan
comments.body:
I did some further research, though unfortunately I still haven't found the solution.

One difference that I spotted between the scripts is the usage of `bnb_4bit_quant_storage`, but even when removed, there is still an error.

Didding deeper, it appears that something goes wrong during the dequantization step:

https://github.com/huggingface/peft/blob/41c274ecac6247a63e3b10f8536904f3ead82213/src/peft/utils/integrations.py#L89

The output is a 2048x2048 shaped float tensor. However, I think it should be a float tensor of shape 2097152x1 because bnb uses flat tensors (and 2097152 == 2048**2 / 2). For reference, I checked the [LoftQ implementation](https://github.com/huggingface/peft/blob/41c274ecac6247a63e3b10f8536904f3ead82213/src/peft/utils/loftq_utils.py#L224) and there I get exactly this flat shape. It is unclear to me why the shapes are different, even though both code paths call `bnb.functional.dequantize_4bit(weight.data, weight.quant_state)`. I checked the `quant_state` too but AFAICT it's the same between the two.

Anyway, because of the wrong shape, we assign an incorrectly shaped (and all zeros) tensor as the new bnb weight here:

https://github.com/huggingface/peft/blob/41c274ecac6247a63e3b10f8536904f3ead82213/src/peft/tuners/lora/layer.py#L189

which is most likely the reason for the shape error later during forward.

When I have time to further investigate, I'll let you know. If any of you have an idea what I'm missing, please let me know.

comments.author: Haakooto
comments.body:
I poked around in the olora_init-function in `peft/src/peft/tuners/lora/layer.py`. As @BenjaminBossan mentions, the difference between my script and the olora-example script is the `bnb_4bit_quant_storage`-flag in the BitsAndBytesConfig. Both scripts crash because of shape-mismatch, both with `bnb_4bit_quant_storage=None` (default) and with `bnb_4bit_quant_storage=torch.bfloat16` (which I used because of [this page](https://huggingface.co/docs/bitsandbytes/main/en/fsdp_qlora)).

However, the relevant shapes are different. As can be seen in the tracebacks posted by me and @BenjaminBossan, with `bnb_4bit_quant_storage=torch.bfloat16`, mat2 has size (1x1), while with `bnb_4bit_quant_storage=None`, it has size (NxM). This is because olora_init does not identify the Linear4bit-instance as quantised as the only check for this is its dtype, which is bfloat16, causing the original weights not to be dequantised before computing the QR-decomposition.

While this does not shed light on the ultimate issue, this is another bug.

github.title: Sampling ~10× slower when using same MCMC object after warmup() vs creating new MCMC with num_warmup=0
github.author: gaetanoscandariato

comments.author: gaetanoscandariato
comments.body:
Hi,

after running some human-intelligence extra tests, I found the problem and here is the artifical-intelligence produced summary:

-------
- Problem: Restarting by creating a new `MCMC(..., num_warmup=0, init_params=...)` *does not* transfer the adapted mass matrix and step size. Only parameter positions are restored. This can produce very fast-looking but *invalid* sampling (high divergence / posterior corruption).
- Root cause: The tuned sampler state is stored in `mcmc.last_state` (contains the adapted mass matrix and step size). `init_params` only sets parameter positions and thus is insufficient for a proper restart.

Minimal reproduction
--------------------
1. Run warmup + sampling on `mcmc = MCMC(NUTS(...))`:
   - `mcmc.warmup(key, ...); mcmc.run(key, ...); last_state = mcmc.last_state`
2. Approach A (problematic):
   - `m2 = MCMC(NUTS(...), num_warmup=0)`
   - `m2.run(key, ..., init_params=last_samples)` → yields many divergences and artificially high it/s (samples are mostly rejected).
3. Approach B (correct):
   - `m2 = MCMC(NUTS(...), num_warmup=0)`
   - `m2.post_warmup_state = last_state; m2._warmup_state = last_state`
   - `m2.run(key, ...)` → normal behaviour (low divergences, proper ESS/rhat).

What we changed
-------------------------
- Save `mcmc.last_state` in checkpoints (pickles) under the key `'mcmc_last_state'` (intermediate + final saves).
- On restart, if `mcmc_last_state` is present, restore it into `mcmc.post_warmup_state` and `mcmc._warmup_state` *before* the first run/batch.
- Added tests verifying both the bad behavior (init_params only → 100% divergences) and the correct restart behavior when state is restored.


Suggested fixes and NumPyro improvements
---------------------------------------
1. Public API for state serialization: provide official helpers to save/restore HMC/NUTS state (mass matrix, step size, adapt info).
2. `MCMC` initialization option for a prior warmup state, e.g. `MCMC(..., initial_state=previous_state)`, or explicit `mcmc.load_state(state)`.
3. Document clearly that `init_params` does *not* include tuning/adaptation state and warn users about unsafe restarts.
4. Provide convenience helpers `mcmc.save_state(path)` / `mcmc.load_state(path)` or analogous utility functions.
5. Consider emitting a warning/error when `num_warmup=0` is used with `init_params` but no sampler state is present.
6. Add diagnostics to highlight suspiciously high iteration rates after restart that coincide with high divergence rates.

Why this matters
-----------------
Users restarting runs with `init_params` (assuming it fully restores sampler state) can unknowingly obtain fast yet invalid sampling and misleading performance numbers. Making the adaptation state explicit and easily restorable avoids silent misuse.

If helpful, I can open a concise issue in the NumPyro repository with the repro script and tests attached, or prepare a prototype PR adding `save_state/load_state` helpers.

Thanks for looking into this.

github.title: Streaming Pipeline Regression in Transformers v5
github.author: davidmezzetti

comments.author: ojasvi24-coder
comments.body: I would love to work on this if it's still open!

comments.author: Sammy-Dabbas
comments.body:
I looked into this and I think I have a fix ready, pending your go-ahead to open a PR.

Root cause: the `inputs = list(inputs)` in `Pipeline.__call__` was added in the v5 chat template change (#42326) so it could read `inputs[0]` to detect chat-style inputs. Generators are not subscriptable, so it materializes the whole thing just to peek at the first element, and on a large or streaming generator that forces the entire stream into memory and OOMs. In v4 there was no such conversion; generators would fall through to the existing lazy `get_iterator` / `PipelineIterator` path.

The fix i have peeks only the first item with `next()`. If it is a chat message, materialize just that single bounded conversation as a `Chat`. Otherwise it  reattach the peeked item to the generator and let it stream through the existing lazy iterator path, so a large generator is never fully materialized. Im avoiding just dropping `GeneratorType` from the container types which is the workaround in the issue, since that silently breaks single-chat-as-generator detection. I have a regression test asserting the generator input is not materialized, and it passes locally.


I also see @ojasvi24-coder offered to take this. Either way, I'm glad to help get this fixed. If you'd like me to open the PR I can do that right away,

comments.author: reallyticsai
comments.body: This issue stems from calling `_shutdown_workers()` directly, which can trigger the underlying PyTorch race condition, especially with large tensors and persistent workers. In production, we've seen similar crashes where PyTorch's internal cleanup via `__del__` suppresses errors, but explicit calls re-expose them, leading to non-zero exit codes. A practical workaround is to patch or override the shutdown routine to catch and suppress exceptions, aligning with PyTorch’s default behavior. Alternatively, you could modify Lightning to conditionally skip `_shutdown_workers()` when running in scenarios similar to your use case. Also, check if upgrading to the latest Lightning version or PyTorch release helps, as there have been ongoing fixes around worker cleanup and shutdown sequences.

comments.author: TheLovesOfLadyPurple
comments.body: @yiyixuxu @sayakpaul @DN6 @asomoza @dg845 @stevhliu

comments.author: dg845
comments.body:
If I understand correctly, the issue is that custom `timesteps` supplied to `FlowMatchEulerDiscreteScheduler.set_timesteps` get desynced from the underlying `sigmas` schedule under certain conditions, the most likely of which is `self.config.shift != 1.0`. (More precisely, they end up no longer satisfying the relationship `sigmas * self.config.num_train_timesteps = timesteps`.) The `timesteps` and `sigmas` start out synced at 

https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers/blob/c4123258d23a89562b6db699ec9136e207bda452/src/diffusers/schedulers/scheduling_flow_match_euler_discrete.py#L341

Since we ultimately create `self.timesteps` from the raw custom `timesteps`:

https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers/blob/c4123258d23a89562b6db699ec9136e207bda452/src/diffusers/schedulers/scheduling_flow_match_euler_discrete.py#L370

if the `sigmas` are modified in between these two lines, for example by shifting (dynamic or not), then the two will no longer be synced. So a smaller reproduction of the issue is as follows:

```python
import torch
from diffusers import FlowMatchEulerDiscreteScheduler

# Create a scheduler with shift != 1.0 (setting other configs like use_karras_sigmas=True would also work)
scheduler = FlowMatchEulerDiscreteScheduler(shift=2.0)
scheduler.set_timesteps(num_inference_steps=10)
torch.testing.assert_close(scheduler.sigmas[:-1] * scheduler.config.num_train_timesteps, scheduler.timesteps)

sigmas = scheduler.sigmas
custom_timesteps = scheduler.timesteps.tolist()
scheduler.set_timesteps(timesteps=custom_timesteps)
# Assertions below fail as the sigmas and timesteps are desynced due to the issue
torch.testing.assert_close(scheduler.sigmas[:-1] * scheduler.config.num_train_timesteps, scheduler.timesteps)
torch.testing.assert_close(sigmas, scheduler.sigmas)
```

An underlying design issue is: should we modify custom `sigmas` or `timesteps` which are supplied to `set_timesteps`? The current code does modify custom `sigmas`, for example by shifting them if shifting is active (which is related to the bug above). On the other hand, I think this behavior might be unexpected (under the assumption that custom timesteps are always honored). @yiyixuxu WDYT?

One case where this behavior matters is that the distilled LTX 2 checkpoints currently need to specify `shift=1.0`, etc. so that the distilled `sigmas` schedule doesn't get modified by `set_timesteps`.

comments.author: dg845
comments.body:
Actually, keeping the current behavior (at least for now) is probably better since this is the way dynamic shifting is usually implemented: most pipelines supply an unshifted custom `sigmas` schedule:

https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers/blob/72eb60c2dad62e44777b5344f21705c6d47bf97f/src/diffusers/pipelines/flux2/pipeline_flux2.py#L934

and expect `FlowMatchEulerDiscreteScheduler.set_timesteps` to do the dynamic shifting using the calculated `mu` value:

https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers/blob/72eb60c2dad62e44777b5344f21705c6d47bf97f/src/diffusers/pipelines/flux2/pipeline_flux2.py#L938-L945

So respecting custom `sigmas` as-is would break this pattern.

> If I understand correctly, the issue is that custom `timesteps` supplied to `FlowMatchEulerDiscreteScheduler.set_timesteps` get desynced from the underlying `sigmas` schedule under certain conditions, the most likely of which is `self.config.shift != 1.0`. (More precisely, they end up no longer satisfying the relationship `sigmas * self.config.num_train_timesteps = timesteps`.) The `timesteps` and `sigmas` start out synced at
> 
> [diffusers/src/diffusers/schedulers/scheduling_flow_match_euler_discrete.py](https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers/blob/c4123258d23a89562b6db699ec9136e207bda452/src/diffusers/schedulers/scheduling_flow_match_euler_discrete.py#L341)
> 
> Line 341 in [c412325](/huggingface/diffusers/commit/c4123258d23a89562b6db699ec9136e207bda452)
> 
>  sigmas = timesteps / self.config.num_train_timesteps 
> Since we ultimately create `self.timesteps` from the raw custom `timesteps`:
