github.title: `LightningDataModule.load_from_checkpoint` does not restore subclass from `datamodule_hyper_parameters`
github.author: aditya0by0

comments.author: GdoongMathew
comments.body:
Hi @aditya0by0, thanks for reporting this issue. 

I don’t have extensive experience with `LightningDataModule`, but from what I can tell, the intention of `load_from_checkpoint` does not seem to be to instantiate any subclasses via the base `LightningDataModule` class. This behavior is consistent with how `LightningModule` works as well.

For instance,
```python
>>> class BoringModule(LightningModule):
...    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
...        ...

>>> BoringModule.load_from_checkpoint(ckpt_path)  # this should work as expected
>>> LightningModule.load_from_checkpoint(ckpt_path)  # this won't work
```

Regarding `cls_spec.varkw` is False, this happens because the inspected `cls_spec` corresponds to `LightningDataModule` rather than the user's custom subclass. If we change same line in 
https://github.com/Lightning-AI/pytorch-lightning/pull/21478/changes#diff-66f006dbadabdd4826bf8fb6dcb776fe4b73871f73daf05f205b6e27aae7a548R1102 to `TestDataSaveHparams.load_from_checkpoint(checkpoint_path)`, then the newly added test cases should pass.

comments.author: aditya0by0
comments.body:
@GdoongMathew , thanks for the detailed response and for taking a look at this.

> This behavior is consistent with how `LightningModule` works as well.

I don’t think this is fully consistent with `LightningModule`. To illustrate this, there is an existing test case that explicitly relies on this behavior:

[https://github.com/Lightning-AI/pytorch-lightning/blob/master/tests/tests_pytorch/test_cli.py#L1069-L1070](https://github.com/Lightning-AI/pytorch-lightning/blob/master/tests/tests_pytorch/test_cli.py#L1069-L1070)

In this test, calling `LightningModule.load_from_checkpoint(...)` correctly instantiates the concrete subclass specified via `_class_path`, even though the base `LightningModule` class is used to invoke `load_from_checkpoint`.

There is also some related discussion here that touches on the same expectation:
[https://github.com/Lightning-AI/pytorch-lightning/discussions/21474](https://github.com/Lightning-AI/pytorch-lightning/discussions/21474)

Coming back to the initially provided reproducible example, if we add the following lines:

```python
model = LightningModule.load_from_checkpoint(checkpoint_path)
assert isinstance(model, TestModelSaveHparams)
```

the assertion passes as expected, which further demonstrates that `LightningModule.load_from_checkpoint` *does* restore the subclass when `_class_path` is present.

This is why the behavior of `LightningDataModule.load_from_checkpoint` felt inconsistent to me, and why I believe the current behavior is a bug rather than an intentional design difference.

Happy to clarify further or adjust the approach if I’m missing something.

comments.author: GdoongMathew
aditya0by0
comments.body:
@GdoongMathew, thanks for the reply.

You’re absolutely right that this is a CLI-specific use case, and that `_instantiator` and `_class_path` are only stored in the checkpoint when using `LightningCLI`. That said, this behavior is still quite valuable in practice: when all model and datamodule classes are already available in the environment, it allows dynamic loading and instantiation at runtime from checkpoint without requiring the user to explicitly reference the concrete class. 

This is especially useful for reproducibility and quick experiment workflows built around the CLI for my use case.

Regarding adding `*args, **kwargs` to `LightningDataModule.__init__`, I don’t think this would introduce issues. `LightningDataModule` and `LightningModule` already share a very similar inheritance structure and both include `HyperparametersMixin` and `DataHooks`:

```python
class LightningDataModule(DataHooks, HyperparametersMixin):
    ...
```

```python
class LightningModule(
    _DeviceDtypeModuleMixin,
    HyperparametersMixin,
    ModelHooks,
    DataHooks,
    CheckpointHooks,
    Module,
):
    ...
```
>I also wouldn’t be opposed to adding *args, **kwargs to LightningDataModule.__init__. If that’s the direction we want to take, I’d be happy to help with the review.

Given this similarity, aligning `LightningDataModule` with `LightningModule` by allowing `*args, **kwargs` in the constructor seems consistent. Hence, I’m happy to proceed with this direction and would appreciate your review on the PR.

github.title: Substantial numerical differences with Minimax MSA attention vs Minimax's Reference
github.author: CoffeeVampir3

comments.author: Charly21r
comments.body:
Thanks for the analysis, I dug into the code and can confirm this. The bug isn't isolated to that one line, the head-collapse is assumed by every consumer of the selection.

## Root cause
[modular_minimax_m3_vl.py:550](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/main/src/transformers/models/minimax_m3_vl/modular_minimax_m3_vl.py#L550):

```
block_scores = scores.amax(dim=-1).amax(dim=1)  # -> [B, S_q, num_key_blocks]
```

scores is `[B, H_idx, S_q, num_key_blocks, block_size]`:
 - `.amax(dim=-1)` pools within the 128-key block
 - .`amax(dim=1)` collapses `H_idx` producing one shared block list per query

The MSA reference's `sparse_topk_select` emits `(total_qo_len, num_qo_heads, topk)` (per-head), where in the MQA-proxy path `max_score.shape[0] == num_kv_heads_real`. With this config `index_n_heads == num_key_value_heads == 4`, so each index head owns one KV group (`qheads_per_kv = 64/4 = 16`). Collapsing the head axis is exactly what drives the ~99.5% selection divergence and the inflated distinct-block count.


It's a shared-selection assumption in 3 places, not one line:
1. Indexer ([modular:550-564](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/main/src/transformers/models/minimax_m3_vl/modular_minimax_m3_vl.py#L550-L564)): collapses heads, returns `[B, S_q, topk]`.
2. eager/sdpa mask ([modular:588](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/main/src/transformers/models/minimax_m3_vl/modular_minimax_m3_vl.py#L588)): build_block_mask does `.unsqueeze(1)`, broadcasting one mask to all query heads.
3. MSA kernel path ([msa_attention.py:204](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/main/src/transformers/integrations/msa_attention.py#L204)): `q2k ... .unsqueeze(0).expand(num_kv_heads, -1, -1)` literally broadcasts the same list to every KV head instead of indexing per head.

So even the kernel path feeds the deployment kernel a head-broadcast selection.

## Proposed fix
 Keep the head axis end-to-end (index head <-> KV head, 1:1):
- `Indexer.forward`: drop `.amax(dim=1)`, keep `block_scores = [B, H_idx, S_q, num_key_blocks]`, and apply the local-block boost and topk per head -> return `[B, H_idx, S_q, topk]`.
- `build_block_mask`: scatter per index head and `repeat_interleave(num_q_heads // H_idx, dim=1)` so it returns `[B, num_q_heads, S_q, S_k]`.
- `_sparse_attention`: replace the `expand(num_kv_heads, …)` with a real per-head reshape, e.g. `q2k = block_indices.permute(1, 0, 2).reshape(num_kv_heads, bsz * q_len, topk)`.

Plus an equivalence test against the reference selection (the overlap metric above is a good basis).

I'm happy to open a PR for this.

github.title: `jnp.std` returns `inf` instead of `nan` for float32 arrays near overflow
github.author: AjBrown89

comments.author: jakevdp
comments.body:
Thanks for the report – I think this is working as expected. `jnp.std` is computed as the square root of the variance, and the variance here is +inf when working at float32 precision.

NumPy's computational model is different: internally it will generally compute things at float64 precision, and this can lead to different numerics in the extreme. For what it's worth, NumPy returns inf in the similar case when operating at the limits of float64 precision:
```python
>>> x = np.array([-1.79769313e+308, 1., 1., 1.79769313e+308])
>>> np.std(x)
/.../numpy/_core/_methods.py:190: RuntimeWarning: overflow encountered in square
np.float64(inf)
```
I'm going to close this, because I think it's working as expected.

comments.author: ernestchu
comments.body: After some investigations, I know the `GradientState` is synced by the **singleton class** design. My current workaround is manually setting `accelerator.gradient_state.end_of_dataloader` to `False` after the evaluation, so the following training would not incorrectly drop samples.

comments.author: sgugger
comments.body: cc @muellerzr

comments.author: muellerzr
comments.body:
@ernestchu `GradientState` is a singleton designed to work with a single dataloader that is currently being iterated upon, which is why you're experiencing this trouble. One thing I could think of is setting an api such as `pause` and `resume` which will "turn off" `GradientState` and/or reset it. So essentially the API would be:

```python
dl1, dl2 = accelerator.prepare(dl1, dl2)
for i,batch in enumerate(dl1):
    ...
    if i == 5:
        accelerator.gradient_state.pause()
        for batch in dl2:
            ....
        accelerator.gradient_state.resume()
    ...
```

Does this seem reasonable to you both @ernestchu @sgugger

The other thought would be just explicitly switching dataloaders, e.g. `accelerator.gradient_state.switch(dl2)`

github.title: [BUG] None grad triggers exception in the backward hook
github.author: eternalNight

comments.author: eternalNight
comments.body: @tohtana Any idea if this two-grad phenomenon is expected? If so, should we add a None check at the beginning of `_backward_prologue_per_tensor`?

comments.author: tohtana
comments.body:
Thank you for reporting, @eternalNight!
I didn't expect the case. Do you think we can simply skip the scaling when the given value is None?

comments.author: eternalNight
comments.body:
> Thank you for reporting, [@eternalNight](https://github.com/eternalNight)! I didn't expect the case. Do you think we can simply skip the scaling when the given value is None?

@tohtana I'll investigate why there is a second grad in the compiled backward graph to see if it is safe to skip `None` grads.

comments.author: eternalNight
comments.body:
@tohtana Here's the story:

1. Llama2 returns a `CausalLMOutputWithPast` (which extends `dict`) which contains a loss tensor (of size 1) and a logits tensor. Deepspeed registers the backward hook on that object, and thus hooks both tensors.
2. Only when DeepCompile is enabled, the backward hooks of both tensors are called, and the hook on logits is called with a `None` grad, probably because it is not scalar.

The hook on logits is not called at all without DeepCompile, regardless of whether torch compile is applied or not. Somehow autograd remembers both tensors and calls their backward hooks before running the backward compile pass.

As `None` grads is caused by non-scalar tensors, I think it is safe to simply skip them in the hook. What do you think?

comments.author: tohtana
comments.body: Thank you @eternalNight for your investigation! Yes, let's simply skip the none grad in the grad. Can you open a PR for it?

comments.author: tohtana
comments.body: @eternalNight Sorry, as I also wanted to run Llama models, I opened #7725. Can you review it? I confirmed it works with Llama-3 7B.

comments.author: rwightman

Also, this isn't trying to delete an old file, at least that callstack is indicating it's during the save & swap part. So to avoid corrupting the previous 'last' checkpoint saved if there was a crash or out of space at the wrong moment, the new checkpoint is first saved to a the `temp.pth.tar`. github.title: Decorating bound methods in profiling utils breaks instance isolation
github.author: ViktoriiaRomanova

comments.author: sayakpaul
comments.body: Is this particular to LTX2 because it has two schedulers?

comments.author: ViktoriiaRomanova
comments.body:
Not specifically. The issue isn’t tied to LTX2 having two schedulers, but rather to the fact that the scheduler is deep-copied inside the `__call__ ` method.

Decorating a bound method freezes the `self` state at decoration time. In addition, without proper rebinding, the <class 'method'> is turned into a plain <class 'function'>, losing its descriptor behaviour. This can lead to a range of issues, especially when instances are copied.

LTX2 just makes the problem more visible, but the underlying issue is general and can occur in any pipeline.

> Is this particular to LTX2 because it has two schedulers?

comments.body:
> Not specifically. The issue isn’t tied to LTX2 having two schedulers, but rather to the fact that the scheduler is deep-copied inside the __call__  method.


Which other pipelines have this pattern?

comments.body:
Under the same conditions (i.e., the scheduler is copied inside the pipeline’s `__call__`), I found the following pipelines that seem to follow this pattern:

* pipeline_skyreels_v2_diffusion_forcing_i2v.py
* pipeline_skyreels_v2_diffusion_forcing_v2v.py
* pipeline_skyreels_v2_diffusion_forcing.py

github.title: Optimizer.step called after on_epoch_end
github.author: RorryB

comments.author: RorryB
comments.body: Just realized this also happens at epoch 0.  So optimizer.step() is called before any data is processed.

comments.author: GdoongMathew
comments.body:
Hi @RorryB , thanks for the report!

From how the hooks are implemented the expected ordering is [`automatic_optimization.run (training_step + optimizer.step)`](https://github.com/Lightning-AI/pytorch-lightning/blob/862314360457fed35672ec9d0c6f5f1998a61eae/src/lightning/pytorch/loops/training_epoch_loop.py#L240) -> [`on_validation_epoch_end`](https://github.com/Lightning-AI/pytorch-lightning/blob/862314360457fed35672ec9d0c6f5f1998a61eae/src/lightning/pytorch/loops/training_epoch_loop.py#L285). Your log output appears to show the same ordering.

Could you share a bit more about whats not working for you or what behavior you expect instead?

comments.author: RorryB
comments.body:
Sure, so I would expect the ordering to be

- Automatic_optimization.run
    - training step
    - optimizer step
    - training step
    - optimizer step
    - ......
    - training step
    - optimizer step
- on validation epoch end

but it looks like it is actually 
- Automatic_optimization.run
    - optimizer step
    - training step
    - optimizer step
    - training step
    - ......
    - training step
- on validation epoch end
- Next automatic optimizer.run
    -  optimizer step

i.e. an optimizer step is called before the first training step, which is also repeated on every training epoch.  and then each training epoch ends with a training step that does not have the optimizer.step actually called until the next training epoch.

It might not be coming through clearly from the log because the optimizer.step print is on the same line as the training bar.  But if you just look at the debugs without the training bar the order is:

DEBUG: training_step start (batch 858)
DEBUG: training_step end (batch 858)
DEBUG: optimizer_step called (epoch 0, batch 859)
DEBUG: training_step start (batch 859)
DEBUG: training_step end (batch 859)
on_validation_epoch_end 
DEBUG: optimizer_step called (epoch 1, batch 0)
DEBUG: training_step start (batch 0)
DEBUG: training_step end (batch 0)

comments.author: GdoongMathew
comments.body:
Thanks for the clarification. So this is actually an expected behavior caused by `lightning` utilizing the closure mechanism in torch optimizer. A reference could be found in this https://github.com/Lightning-AI/pytorch-lightning/pull/21120#issuecomment-3227587883 as well.

Basically, `lightning` wraps the work from `training_step` through `on_before_optimizer_step` into one big closure function and passes that to `optimizer.step` argument. Optimizer would call that closure internally ([ref](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/torch/optim/sgd.py#L114-L116)). That's why the logs can look like `optimizer.step` runs before `training_step`, but the training logic inside the closure is still executed before the actual parameter update.

comments.author: RorryB
comments.body:
Im not sure if I follow.  From your referenced comment:

# closure function for optimizer
            strategy.training_step()
            └── LightningModule.training_step()

            callback.on_before_zero_grad()
            LightningModule.on_before_zero_grad()
            LightningModule.optimizer_zero_grad()
            strategy.backward()
            ├── callback.on_before_backward()
            ├── LightningModule.on_before_backward()
            ├── LightningModule.backward()
            │   └── loss.backward()
            ├── callback.on_after_backward()
            └── LightningModule.on_after_backward()

            callback.on_before_optimizer_step()
            LightningModule.on_before_optimizer_step()
            LightningModule.configure_gradient_clipping()
    
            optimizer.step(closure)

It still looks like that (training_step through on_before_optimizer_step) is fully called before optimizer.step.  I don't understand why the logs would make it look like optimizer.step() is running first if it is not.  My actual use case where i found this is also more complex than just printing the logs and it was causing things to crash. I can try to add complexity to this minimum example to cause the same effect with more than just print statements.

comments.author: GdoongMathew
comments.body:
So, at a high level, the pseudo-code for the optimizer closure looks like this:

```python
def closure():
    LightningModule.training_step()
    LightningModule.optimizer_zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    LightningModule.on_before_optimizer_step()

optimizer.step(closure=closure)
```

If you add a debug print before and after the `optimizer.step`

```python
class LightningMNISTClassifier(pl.LightningModule):
    def optimizer_step(self, epoch, batch_idx, optimizer, optimizer_closure):
        print(f"DEBUG: optimizer_step called (epoch {epoch}, batch {batch_idx})", flush=True)
        optimizer.step(closure=optimizer_closure)    # --> The `training_step` is included in the `optimizer_closure` here
        print(f"DEBUG: optimizer_step called finished (epoch {epoch}, batch {batch_idx})", flush=True)
```

Then you should see logs similar to the following:
```text
DEBUG: optimizer_step called (epoch 0, batch 858)
DEBUG: training_step start (batch 858)
DEBUG: training_step end (batch 858)
DEBUG: optimizer_step called finished (epoch 0, batch 858)
```
 which shows the training step is executed within the optimizer step via the provided closure, rather than being called separately afterward.

comments.author: RorryB
comments.body:
Awesome, thank you for this detailed explanation!  This helped me track down my bug.  I've never seen this step(closure) idea before.  

FYI, and If anyone else looks at this later with the same problem, I have fairly complicated setup for my project that does some other stuff before the step().  My usual order without Lightning is training step -> zero grad -> other stuff -> optimizer step.  But closure was re ordering it to be other stuff -> training step -> zero grad -> optimizer step.  By taking this closure concept into account I was able to rearrange where my other stuff is running and get things in the right order.

Thanks again!

github.author: shunmian

comments.author: rwightman
comments.body:
@shunmian that's not augmentation, that's expected cropping. The transforms output a constant image size, it defaults to square unless you provide a different size tuple. You input a non-square image it resizes the shortest size to 224 and then crops center to output 224 x 224. Not sure what else you would expect, this is the default preprocessing expected for most models. Note the scale/ratio args are for training random resize & crop and don't impact things when is_training=False.

If you want the whole image you can specificy `crop_mode='squash'`, but it will distort aspect, or `crop_mode=border` and it will add borders (letterboxing) to achieve target size.
